title: Folio 8: The Nomads Who Asked for a Little Land
description: They came out of the desert with their tents and their herds, and they asked the sultan for a few dry pastures. Within three years they were sitting on his throne in Nishapur. This is how the Seljuqs, a small band of Turkmen nomads, arrived at the edge of the Ghaznavid empire, and how a proud sultan failed to take them seriously.
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi, the volumes on the years 426 to 429 AH (1035 to 1038 CE): the Seljuq letters to the court, the defeat of the chamberlain Begtoghdi near Nasa, the grant of Nasa, Farawa and Dihistan, Amir Masud's vow to take Hansi and his ministers' objections, and the loss of Nishapur; Beyhaqi's statement of method in the same work; background from Encyclopaedia Iranica, Britannica and Wikipedia ('Arslan Isra'il', 'Tughril I', 'Chaghri Beg', 'Begtoghdi', 'Battle of Nasa (1035)', 'Mas'ud I of Ghazni')
cold_open: A letter arrives at the sultan's court. It comes from a band of nomads at the edge of the desert. They call themselves the sultan's servants, and they ask for only a little land, enough for their flocks. Three years later, one of those nomads will sit on the sultan's own throne.
paragraphs: Welcome to The Honest Historian. I'm Mehdi Rahmani, and this is Folio Eight. Today a new people rides into our story. They arrive with tents, horses and sheep, and they ask the sultan for a few dry pastures.
The sultan thinks they are a small problem. He is wrong. They are the Seljuqs, and within a generation they will rule from Central Asia to the borders of Byzantium.

Let us start far to the north, on the open steppe beyond the great river the Greeks called the Oxus. Here lived the Oghuz, Turkish tribes who moved with the seasons. Their wealth was not in cities or treasuries. It was in their horses, their sheep and their skill with the bow.

Among them was a chief named Seljuq. Around the end of the tenth century, his clan moved south toward the towns of the Muslim world, and they became Muslims. Seljuq had sons. One was called Mikail. Another was called Arslan, who is better known by his other name, Israil.

Mikail had two sons of his own, and you should remember their names, because they are the heroes of this story, or its villains, depending on where you stand. One was Tughril. The other was Chaghri. Both names belong to birds of prey. Chaghri means something like a small falcon. They grew up as raiders and soldiers for hire, fighting for whichever Turkish prince on the Oxus would pay them.
From their own point of view, they were not invaders yet. They were a hungry clan looking for grass, water and a safe place to live.
The first meeting between the Seljuqs and the house of Ghazni ended badly for the Seljuqs.

In the year ten twenty five, the great Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni crossed the Oxus. The Turkish princes of the north were his rivals, and the Seljuqs fought among their allies. The sources do not agree on exactly how it happened. Some say Arslan Israil was taken in battle. Others say he was invited to talks and arrested. Either way, Mahmud now held the leader of the clan.

He sent Arslan Israil far away, to a mountain fortress called Kalinjar, in northern India. There, it seems, Arslan spent the rest of his life as a prisoner. He died in captivity around the year ten thirty two.

But Mahmud did something else, something that later writers would argue about for centuries. Some of Arslan's Turkmen followers asked for permission to cross into Khorasan, the rich eastern province of Iran. Mahmud allowed them to settle on the edges of the desert, near the towns of Sarakhs, Farawa and Abivard. He hoped, perhaps, to use them as soldiers.

Not everyone agreed. Arslan Jadhib, Mahmud's governor at Tus, warned his master that these nomads would bring trouble. Mahmud brushed the warning aside. And soon enough, the Turkmen began to raid villages and roads. In the end Mahmud had to come himself to Khorasan and give Arslan Jadhib an army to drive them out. The old governor had been right.

Mahmud died in ten thirty. His son Masud became sultan, and Masud is the main character of Beyhaqi's history. You have met him already in this series: brave, generous, clever, and very sure of himself.

Meanwhile, Tughril and Chaghri were still on the move. For a while they served the governor of Khwarazm, the land on the lower Oxus near the Aral Sea. Then, in ten thirty five, a rival Turkish lord named Shah Malik fell upon them and killed many of their people. The clan was suddenly homeless.
So they did something bold. They crossed the desert south into Khorasan and came to the town of Nasa, at the foot of the mountains. And they wrote to the sultan.

Beyhaqi had a special view of this moment. He worked in the royal chancery, the office that wrote and read the sultan's letters, under his teacher Bu Nasr Moshkan. So the letters of these nomads passed through rooms he knew well.

The message, as Beyhaqi reports it, was humble. The Seljuqs called themselves the sultan's servants. They had nowhere to go, they said. They asked to be given the dry lands around Nasa and Farawa for their flocks. In return they would guard the frontier and keep other nomads out. They were even ready, it seems, to send one of their own as a hostage.
To a careful ruler, this might have been an opportunity. To Masud, it was an insult. Who were these shepherds to ask for land in his province? His answer was an army.

In the summer of ten thirty five, a large Ghaznavid force marched toward Nasa. Its commander was a senior chamberlain named Begtoghdi, an old Turkish officer of the court. Modern historians put his army at around fifteen thousand men. These were trained soldiers, with heavy equipment and baggage.

At first, things seemed to go well. The Seljuqs gave ground. But this was the oldest trick of the steppe. Nomad riders would pretend to run, wait for the enemy to break ranks and scatter, and then turn and strike.

According to the accounts that come down to us, the Ghaznavid soldiers lost their discipline, some of them busy with the Seljuq camp and its goods. Then the Seljuqs came back. The sultan's army was beaten and fled. Another senior officer was captured.

Now Masud had to choose. For the moment, he chose to talk. He agreed to what the nomads had asked for in the first place. Nasa, Farawa and Dihistan were given to the Seljuq leaders. In return they promised to obey the sultan. Robes of honour and letters of appointment were sent to them, as if they were loyal servants of the state.
On paper, the Seljuqs were now the sultan's men. In reality, everyone had learned something. The nomads had learned that the great army of Ghazni could be beaten.

You might ask how we know so much about these quarrels, a thousand years later. The answer is that Beyhaqi made a promise to his readers. In one famous passage, he explains his rule for writing history. In his Persian it goes something like this:
Ya az moayene-ye man ast, ya az sama-e dorost az mardi seqe.
It means: what I write is either something I saw with my own eyes, or something I heard correctly from a trustworthy man.
That is why his account of these years feels so close. He is not telling a legend. He is telling what came across his desk, and what the men around him said in the corridors of the court.

Over the next two years, the frontier became a wound that would not close. The Seljuqs did not stay quietly in their pastures. Their bands raided further into Khorasan. Towns paid them to go away. Merv, one of the great cities of the region, slipped from the sultan's control. Tax money stopped coming in.
And what was Sultan Masud doing? He was thinking about India.
Masud made a vow to capture a famous fortress in northern India called Hansi. His father Mahmud had won glory and enormous treasure in India, and Masud wanted the same.

Beyhaqi tells us that his ministers tried hard to stop him. Their argument, in our own words, was simple. If Khorasan is lost to the Turkmen while you are away, then even ten victories in India will not make up for it.

Masud would not listen. He had made a vow, and he would keep it. In the autumn of ten thirty seven he marched east, and early in the next year, Hansi fell to him. It was a real victory. But it was a victory in the wrong place.
While Masud was far away in the east, the north fell apart.

In ten thirty eight, a Ghaznavid army was badly defeated near Sarakhs. Now the road to Nishapur lay open. Nishapur was the capital of Khorasan, a wealthy city of scholars and merchants. Its leading men looked at the situation and made a hard decision. There was no army to defend them. Better to open the gates than to see the city sacked.

First came Ibrahim Inal, a half brother of Tughril, with only a small band of riders. At Friday prayers, the sermon was read in the name of Tughril. In the Islamic world, this was the clearest sign of who ruled a city.

Then Tughril himself arrived. He was received in the sultan's garden palace outside the city, called Shadyakh. And there, the sources say, the nomad chief sat down on the throne that had been prepared for Sultan Masud.
Think about that for a moment. Only three years earlier, this man had written to the sultan, calling himself a servant and asking for a little grazing land. Now he sat on that same sultan's throne.

Beyhaqi does not tell this story to make fun of the Seljuqs. He tells it to show how a great power can lose a province without one single great battle. It happened through pride, through a refusal to listen, and through a sultan who looked at a hungry clan of herders and saw only shepherds.
If there is one lesson here, it is this: never measure a danger by how humble it looks at your door.

Next week, Masud finally turns to face the Seljuqs with all his strength. Elephants, tens of thousands of soldiers, and a desert fortress called Dandanqan. It is the battle of ten forty, the day the Ghaznavid empire broke in Khorasan.

If you enjoyed this story, follow the show so you don't miss the next one, and share it with someone who loves history. I'm Mehdi Rahmani. This episode was retold from the Persian original of the History of Beyhaqi, and narrated with an AI rendering of my own voice. Thank you for listening.
